newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU MAY CLEAR SHIP AID IN GERMANY, GREECE, SPAIN.
newsitem.headline: EU MAY CLEAR SHIP AID IN GERMANY, GREECE, SPAIN.

text.p: European Union industry ministers are likely to give the green light this week to state aid to ailing German, Spanish and Greek shipyards despite opposition from some member states, EU diplomats said on Monday.

But the outcome of Thursday's ministerial meeting in Luxembourg remains uncertain. The EU's three Nordic members and Britain, traditionally critical of state subsidies, have expressed strong doubts about the restructuring aid.

The European Commission's proposal to approve the requests of Bonn, Athens and Madrid to grant the support, which has sparked U.S. criticism, needs the backing of a qualified majority of EU member states.
"I'd give it a 60 percent chance," one EU diplomat said.
Other diplomats and officials appeared more confident that the three governments would be able to go ahead with the aid.
"I assume that the Council of Ministers will approve it," EU Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann said last week.
But Sweden, the only country so far to put its cards on the table, has said it will vote against.
Somewhat ironically, the expected decision comes at a time when the 15-nation bloc is strongly urging the United States to ratify an international deal to slash support to the sector.
The EU executive had delayed a decision on the ship aid, waiting for U.S. ratification of the deal struck through the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
But it decided to go ahead with its proposal to EU industry ministers after a meeting last month of the OECD, the club of wealthy industrial nations, failed to produce an outcome.
However, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert tried to ease concerns among other shipbuilders, saying the aid would not significantly boost the yards' competitive position.
Germany, Spain and Greece had undertaken not to pay any more rescue or restructuring aid to the shipyards.
The EU executive also insisted on important reductions in production capacity in Germany and Spain and there would be strict monitoring of the conditions imposed on the shipyards.
The German aid would help two shipyards in former east Germany previously owned by bankrupt Bremer Vulkan .
The problems of MTW-Schiffswerft and Volkswerft Stralsund arose from alleged misuse by Bremer Vulkan of 850 million marks ($500 million) in subsidies intended for them.
Of the needed aid of around one billion marks, 728 million marks would require the approval of EU industry ministers.
In Greece, the proposal would allow Athens to write off 54.5 billion drachmas ($201 million) in debts accumulated by Hellenic shipyards before it was privatised in 1995.

The Spanish support was needed for restructuring public yards to return them to viability by the end of 1998. A large part of the proposed aid, 180 billion pesetas ($1.25 billion), was provided for in an exemption for Spain under the OECD deal.
But a further 135 billion pesetas in interest payments, tax credits and capital injection were also needed.

EU officials insist the proposed aid would have been allowed also if the OECD deal had been in force. That accord is designed to end direct shipbuilding subsidies except social aid, and research and development aid.
Due to difficulties in the Republican-controlled Congress, the United States is the only country which has not yet ratified the 1994 accord within the 29-nation OECD.
Among other things, U.S. shipyards argue they have not had enough time to adjust to the commercial era after the loss of military contracts at the end of the Cold War.
Despite the delay, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky last month expressed "dismay" at the proposal by the EU executive to clear the aid in Germany, Greece and Spain.
Van Miert dismissed the criticism, noting that the EU, unlike the United States, had ratified the OECD deal in time.
($1 = 270 drachmas)
($1 = 143.9 pesetas)
